summary:
Yukon is a territory of Canada. Its own human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination, covering employment, housing, and public and private accommodation.

Legal change of gender is available in Yukon. Birth certificates and other vital-statistics documents fall under territorial jurisdiction, and the sources reviewed do not set out Yukon's own requirements for amending a marker.

On 30 March 2026 the Yukon Legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility, with members rising to speak across party lines. Yukon Party MLA Wade Istchenko (Kluane) praised the courage, resilience and contributions of transgender, two-spirited and gender-diverse Yukoners, stated that too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment and hate for far too long, and cited a national study finding that transgender people aged 15 to 17 face 7.6 times the risk of a suicide attempt. The tribute places cross-party legislative acknowledgement of trans residents on Yukon's public record.
tangentialFactors:
Statistics Canada's release Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024, published 30 March 2026, records 4,882 police-reported hate crimes nationally in 2024, up 1% on 2023 and 169% on 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents motivated by gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive yearly increase and 184% above the 2020 level. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, though June 2024 alone accounted for 113 incidents against a monthly average of roughly 50 across the year. These are national totals with no Yukon breakdown, and the release ranks nothing on a per-capita territorial basis.

The same release puts police-reported hate-crime rates at 13.9 per 100,000 in large metropolitan areas against 5.5 in smaller towns. That gap bears on a sparsely populated territory where reporting infrastructure is thinner, but the sources do not show how the national pattern applies within Yukon.

A Pride flag was allegedly vandalised and stolen from Holy Family Elementary School in the Porter Creek neighbourhood of Whitehorse over a weekend in June 2024, and a replacement was put up promptly. In a statement issued 12 June 2024, Yukon Education Minister Jeanie McLean reaffirmed her commitment to the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity education policy, SOGI 123.
localsOnly:
The 30 March 2026 tribute was delivered on the floor of the Yukon Legislature, so cross-party recognition of trans, two-spirited and gender-diverse Yukoners, together with an acknowledgement of discrimination and hate experienced by them, is on the territorial public record.

Yukon schools operate under the territory's sexual orientation and gender identity policy, SOGI 123, which the education minister publicly reaffirmed on 12 June 2024 in response to the flag incident at Holy Family Elementary School. Residents amending a vital-statistics marker do so under territorial jurisdiction over those documents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources reviewed do not set out Yukon's own requirements for amending a gender marker on a birth certificate or other vital-statistics document. Territorial jurisdiction over those documents is established; the applicable procedure is not sourced.

Not sourced: no Yukon-level hate-crime or victimisation figures appear anywhere in the inventory. The Statistics Canada release and the Egale Canada 2024 hate-crime analysis are both national and neither reports territory-level data, so neither can be read as a Yukon prevalence figure.

Unresolved: the 7.6-times suicide-attempt risk quoted in the legislature on 30 March 2026 derives from a national study of transgender people aged 15 to 17, not a Yukon sample, and the sources give no survey period for it.

Not sourced: whether Yukon's own police-reported data record gender-motivated incidents, and how Yukon human rights complaints alleging gender-identity discrimination have been handled, are not documented in the inventory.
